---
title: "6.1 Lift and drag from Bernoulli?"
---

{{< include ../_checkpoint-widget.qmd >}}

## The big idea

Can Bernoulli tell us the force a flow puts on an object? Lift on a wing, drag on a lamppost in a windstorm... these are the numbers engineers actually get paid for.

We'll use two ingredients: Bernoulli tells us how pressure changes as the flow speeds up and slows down around an object; then, from hydrostatics, we know how to turn a pressure distribution into a force.

(A warning! The answer we get is famously wrong! But the example is instructive, and the technique is still useful in other examples.)

## Think first

**Recall**

1. Bernoulli's Equation: $p+\frac12 \rho U^2 +\rho g z =\text{ constant}$ along a streamline.
2. The force from pressure on a surface: $\mathbf{F}=\int -p(\mathbf{x})\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA$, with $\hat{\mathbf{n}}$ pointing from the surface into the fluid.

**Look ahead**

1. Wind blows past a round lamppost. Where on the lamppost's surface do you think the air moves fastest? Where is the pressure highest?
2. Does the pressure on the back of the lamppost end up higher or lower than on the front?
3. Suppose the pressure on the surface turned out to be perfectly symmetric, front-to-back. What would that say about the drag?


## The setup

Let's think about flow around a cylinder — here's the picture:

Uniform flow with speed $U_0$, pressure $p_0$, and density $\rho$ approaches a cylinder of radius $R$ and large width $W$. We choose to define $\theta=0$ at the back of the cylinder.

Our goal is to determine the lift (vertical force) and drag (horizontal force) on this cylinder. We will do so by figuring out the pressure on the surface of the cylinder, and, thinking back to hydrostatics, we can integrate pressure to get force.

The diagram above includes one streamline that goes from upstream (state "0") to an arbitrary location on the surface of the cylinder  (state "x"). Write Bernoulli:

$$
p_0 + \frac12 \rho U_0^2 + \rho g z_0 = p(\mathbf{x}) + \frac12 \rho U(\mathbf{x})^2 + \rho g z(\mathbf{x})
$$

where $U(\mathbf{x}) = |\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x})|$ is the speed at our location $\mathbf{x}$. We'll assume the change in elevation is negligible, then rearrange to get

$$
p(\mathbf{x}) = p_0 + \frac12 \rho U_0^2 - \frac12\rho\left[U(\mathbf{x})\right]^2
$$

So... if we know the speed everywhere on the surface, we know the pressure everywhere on the surface. We need the **velocity field**.


## The velocity field around a cylinder

In 2D cylindrical coordinates, the flow around the cylinder is

$$
\begin{aligned}
u_r(r,\theta) &= U_0\left(1-\frac{R^2}{r^2}\right)\cos\theta \\
u_\theta(r,\theta) &= -U_0\left(1+\frac{R^2}{r^2}\right)\sin\theta.
\end{aligned}
$$

This is a result from **potential flow theory** (something you might see in graduate fluid mechanics) and is written in terms of the radial and angular components of velocity: $u_r$ is the component of velocity moving away from the origin, $u_\theta$ is the component moving counter-clockwise around the origin.

A couple of sanity checks:

- Far from the cylinder, $r \gg r$, and so $u_r \to U_0\cos\theta$ and $u_\theta \to -U_0 \sin\theta$. Above the cylinder, $\theta=\pi/2$, so these components become $u_r =0$ and $u_\theta=-U_0$ (as expected).
- Upstream of the cylinder, $\theta=\pi$ and $u_r=U_0$ and $u_\theta=0$ (as expected).
- On the surface, $r=R$ and $u_r=0$ (as expected... the flow can't go through the surface.
- Also on the surface, $u_\theta = -2U_0 \sin \theta$. Hmm...


::: {.callout-important}
In our derivation of Bernoulli's Equation, we assumed $\mu\approx 0$... that is, we ignored viscosity. Because of this, we cannot use the *no-slip condition* when doing analyses in this regime. We have here that $u_\theta(R,\theta) \neq 0$... there is slip on the surface of this sphere.

Later, we'll talk about how there is a thin boundary layer that forms very near the surface, and within this boundary layer we have the speed reduced to zero. This layer is thin, so the velocity profile above is decent in most of the fluid.
:::

Since we are thinking about the pressure and velocity on the surface, we can focus on

$$
u_r(R,\theta) = 0, \qquad u_\theta(R,\theta) = -2U_0\sin\theta.
$$

A **stagnation point** is a place where the flow comes to a complete stop: *both* velocity components are zero. Where are they on this cylinder?

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="One stagnation point is on the front of the cylinder, where the oncoming flow hits it head-on. At what angle θ is it, in degrees?"
     data-answer="180" data-tol="0.02" data-units="°"
     data-hint="On the surface u_r = 0 everywhere, so you only need u_θ = −2U₀ sin θ = 0. Also remember where θ = 0 is: the back of the cylinder, on the +x axis."
     data-solution="We need sin θ = 0, so θ = 0 or θ = 180°. The front of the cylinder (facing the oncoming flow, on the −x axis) is θ = 180°."
     data-target="ld-gate-stag-front"></div>
```

::: {#ld-gate-stag-front .fl-hidden}
Right, $\theta = 180°$. The oncoming flow has to decide whether to go over or under, and exactly at the nose it does neither (just like the front of the Pitot tube).

```{=html}
<div class="fl-checkpoint"
     data-prompt="The same equation predicts a second stagnation point. Where is it? Give θ in degrees, between 0 and 359."
     data-answer="0" data-tol="0.02" data-units="°"
     data-hint="sin θ = 0 has two solutions between 0 and 359°. You already found one."
     data-solution="sin θ = 0 at θ = 0 as well: the very back of the cylinder, on the downstream side."
     data-target="ld-gate-stag-back"></div>
```
:::

::: {#ld-gate-stag-back .fl-hidden}
$\theta = 0$: the **back** of the cylinder. The flow speeds up to $2U_0$ over the shoulders ($\theta = \pm 90°$), then slows all the way back down to zero on the downstream side, so it's symmetric front-to-back. The front stagnation point is what we'd expect. The back one is a little suspicious, so let's keep it in mind...
:::







## The pressure on the surface

Now we can write

$$
p(R,\theta) = p_0 + \frac12\rho U_0^2 - \frac12\rho\left[-2U_0\sin\theta\right]^2
= p_0 + \frac12 \rho U_0^2\left(1-4\sin^2\theta\right)
$$


::: {.column-margin}
Sometimes this is reported as the dimensionless **pressure coefficient**,

$$
C_p \equiv \frac{p - p_0}{\frac12\rho U_0^2} = 1 - 4\sin^2\theta,
$$

which conveniently doesn't depend on $U_0$, $\rho$, or $R$ at all.
:::


which we can use in a force-from-pressure equation, just as we did with hydrostatics 

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbf{F} &= -\iint p(\mathbf{x})\,\hat{\mathbf{n}}(\mathbf{x})\,dA \\
&= -\int_0^W\!\!\int_0^{2\pi}\left[p_0 + \frac12\rho U_0^2\left(1-4\sin^2\theta\right)\right]\left<\cos\theta,\sin\theta\right> a\,d\theta\,dz.
\end{aligned}
$$

Here, the surface normal of the cylinder points radially outward, $\hat{\mathbf{n}} = \hat{\mathbf{r}} = \left<\cos\theta, \sin\theta\right>$ in Cartesian components, and on the curved wall, $dA = R\,d\theta\,dz$.


::: {.column-margin}
Careful: $z$ here is the coordinate *along the cylinder's axis* (into the page), not elevation.
:::

The $x$-component is the force along the flow direction, the **drag**. The $y$-component is the force perpendicular to the flow, the **lift**.

You can evaluate this integral yourself to prove it, but it turns out that **both the $\hat{x}$- and $\hat{y}$-components of the force are zero**!

Why is this? The zero lift we might have expected: there is nothing to break the symmetry, so there is no reason for the cylinder to be pushed up or down.

But zero drag is harder to rationalize. It turns out that the solution I gave you is symmetric in the $x$-direction as well — there is some "push" on the leading edge and, at least according to this potential flow theory, there is a matching push on the trailing edge as well. This result is called **d'Alembert's Paradox** (from 1752). It's a "paradox" because anyone who has stuck their hand out of a car window knows that it's wrong.


## What went wrong: wakes

Bernoulli's Equation (and potential flow) does not predict **wakes**. Here's what flow around a cylinder actually looks like:

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 1.5em 0;">
<svg width="560" height="240" viewBox="0 0 560 240" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
  <!-- opaque background so the diagram stays legible in dark mode too -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="560" height="240" fill="#ffffff"/>

  <!-- the flow hugs the front of the cylinder... -->
  <g fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="2" stroke-linecap="round">
    <path d="M 60 70 C 140 70 170 50 220 48 C 250 47 262 58 270 66"/>
    <path d="M 60 170 C 140 170 170 190 220 192 C 250 193 262 182 270 174"/>
    <path d="M 60 105 C 120 105 150 80 185 70"/>
    <path d="M 60 135 C 120 135 150 160 185 170"/>
  </g>

  <!-- the cylinder -->
  <circle cx="220" cy="120" r="60" fill="#c9c6c2" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- ...and then lets go, leaving a messy wake behind it -->
  <g fill="none" stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linecap="round">
    <path d="M 270 66 C 300 60 330 70 350 62 C 370 55 390 72 410 64"/>
    <path d="M 270 174 C 300 180 330 170 350 178 C 370 185 390 168 410 176"/>
    <path d="M 290 90 c 18 -14 38 -2 30 14 c -8 16 -30 10 -24 -4"/>
    <path d="M 300 145 c 16 16 38 6 32 -10 c -6 -16 -28 -12 -24 2"/>
    <path d="M 350 105 c 14 -12 32 0 24 14 c -8 14 -26 6 -20 -6"/>
    <path d="M 360 140 c 12 12 30 4 26 -10 c -4 -12 -22 -10 -18 2"/>
    <path d="M 410 100 c 12 -10 26 0 20 12 c -6 12 -22 6 -16 -4"/>
    <path d="M 420 138 c 10 10 26 4 22 -8 c -4 -10 -18 -8 -14 2"/>
    <path d="M 460 118 c 10 -8 22 0 16 10 c -6 10 -18 4 -12 -4"/>
  </g>

</svg>
</div>
```


The flow follows the front of the cylinder more-or-less like Bernoulli says. But at a certain point, the flow can't turn as quickly as the geometry (due to inertia) and the flow **separates** from the surface, creating a swirling low-pressure wake. We have an asymmetric 

The culprit is viscosity, which we threw out when we used Bernoulli. It turns out that even a tiny bit of viscosity, in a very thin layer right next to the wall, is enough to cause the separation (it is genuinely strange that a *tiny* viscosity can matter this much, and we'll come back to it when we get to boundary layers). So **the above analysis is dubious for blunt objects.**

::: {.callout-warning}
## Don't take this home

"Bernoulli says drag is zero" is *not* a result to carry into a design. It's a result about what Bernoulli leaves out. For a blunt object like a cylinder, a sphere, a lamppost, or a truck, the drag is mostly due to the wake, and we will need a different set of tools (and experimental data) to predict it.
:::


## Airfoils

However — airfoils are **streamlined** (they make very little wake) and **asymmetric**:

```{=html}
<div style="display:flex; justify-content:center; margin: 1.5em 0;">
<svg width="620" height="200" viewBox="0 0 620 200" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" font-family="sans-serif">
  <defs>
    <marker id="af-arrow-blue" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#2b6ca3"/>
    </marker>
    <marker id="af-arrow-red" viewBox="0 0 10 10" refX="9" refY="5" markerWidth="6" markerHeight="6" orient="auto-start-reverse">
      <path d="M 0 0 L 10 5 L 0 10 z" fill="#c0392b"/>
    </marker>
  </defs>

  <!-- opaque background so the diagram stays legible in dark mode too -->
  <rect x="0" y="0" width="620" height="200" fill="#ffffff"/>

  <!-- oncoming flow, tilted slightly: the wing meets it at an angle of attack -->
  <g stroke="#2b6ca3" stroke-width="2" marker-end="url(#af-arrow-blue)">
    <line x1="30" y1="90"  x2="130" y2="80"/>
    <line x1="30" y1="125" x2="130" y2="115"/>
    <line x1="30" y1="160" x2="130" y2="150"/>
  </g>

  <!-- the airfoil: round nose, curved top, flatter bottom, sharp trailing edge -->
  <path d="M 190 125 C 190 100 230 88 290 86 C 380 84 480 110 560 142
           C 480 132 380 140 290 146 C 230 150 190 145 190 125 Z"
        fill="#c9c6c2" stroke="#1a1a1a" stroke-width="2"/>

  <!-- the net result -->
  <line x1="370" y1="95" x2="370" y2="28" stroke="#c0392b" stroke-width="2.2" marker-end="url(#af-arrow-red)"/>
  <text x="380" y="44" font-size="17" fill="#c0392b" xml:space="preserve"><tspan font-style="italic">F</tspan><tspan font-size="11" dy="4">L</tspan><tspan font-size="17" dy="-4"> &gt; 0</tspan></text>
</svg>
</div>
```

Streamlined means the flow follows the surface all the way to the back — no big separated wake — and so Bernoulli is a much better description of the flow here than it was for the cylinder. We *still* get $F_D = 0$ from this analysis (d'Alembert doesn't go away!), but for a streamlined shape the real drag really is small, so that's not a terrible approximation. And because the shape (and its angle to the flow) is asymmetric, the top-bottom cancellation we saw for the cylinder doesn't happen: the flow moves faster over the top, the pressure is lower there, and we get $F_L > 0$.

::: {.column-margin}
I'm skipping a subtle piece here: to get lift out of potential flow, you also need to add some "circulation" to the flow around the wing, and the sharp trailing edge is what picks how much (the *Kutta condition*, if you want to read more). This is a nice example of the math not being able to decide something on its own, and the physics of the real, slightly-viscous flow stepping in to decide it.
:::

::: {.callout-caution}
## A popular wrong explanation

You may have heard that the air over the top of a wing goes faster because it "has further to travel" and needs to "meet back up" with the air underneath at the trailing edge. The faster-on-top part is right. The meet-back-up part is not — there's no rule that says the two parcels have to arrive together (and in real measurements, the air over the top actually gets to the trailing edge *first*). Bernoulli connects the speed to the pressure; it doesn't explain *why* the speed is higher on top.
:::
